items.title: We Must Always Remain Thankful For The Dallas Cowboys
items.author: Tom Ley
items.content:
This year's slate of Thanksgiving games couldn't have unfolded much better from the perspective of a neutral fan. It was hard not to feel stuffed after just the first game, a 39-35 Bears win over the Lions that featured some of the season's most entertaining football, being played by two of the league's most entertaining teams. How could a game like that possibly be topped? Perhaps with a game that was just as thrilling, featured a 21-point comeback, provided a healthy dose of schadenfreude. That is what the Eagles and Cowboys delivered in the second game of the day: a purely delightful viewing experience.

I am always left with a slight sickly feeling at the end of a game like Bears-Lions, only because it feels unfair for a game so good to have to produce a loser. It just doesn't seem right that Jahmyr Gibbs can carry the ball 21 times for 205 yards and three touchdowns, and not get to spend today as the biggest story in the NFL. This is why the Cowboys are such a valuable presence in the league: They could come out on the losing end of the greatest game of all time, and not one person, save for some number of degenerates, would be forced to feel an ounce of sympathy for them. Reasons to delight in the suffering of this franchise are so myriad that everyone can find their own for doing so (I choose this one).

The Dallas Cowboys of recent vintage have become especially adept at delivering the goods to their true constituents, the nation's haters. A team with this purpose must maintain a delicate balance. They can't be so bad as to make all of their games unwatchable, but they can't be good enough to find steady competence. They have to be both an entertaining watch and a squad of self-sabotaging dopes. For a while there, we all had to wait until the playoffs for the Cowboys to make their face-first landing, but now the team has been fine-tuned to meet their true purpose. We can watch the Cowboys eat shit in inventive, entertaining ways just about every week now.

items.title: After The Feast
items.author: Ray Ratto
items.content:
Thanksgiving Day has been a fully owned subsidiary of the National Football League since the 1960s, and a feature of the schedule since the early '20s, but there is an American tradition older than the Dayton Triangles and Frankford Yellow Jackets, and that's turning on your boss.

In other words, Aaron Rodgers stole the weekend before it even started, and thoughtfully if coincidentally, the three teams that Rodgers claimed Mike McCarthy inflicted his narcoleptic cruelties upon, the Green Bay Packers, Dallas Cowboys and Pittsburgh Steelers, featured heavily.

items.title: Rivalry Week Is Here To Ruin Some Postseason Plans
items.author: Ray Ratto
items.content:
It's seeds-and-stems time in the college football season, and if that only means something for you older stoners, a glimpse at the schedule should tell you just how desirable that is. It's Rivalry Week for those schools that have a natural rival, and plain old Week The Last for everyone else. But even the rivalry games don't burn the way they used to. Indiana is now light years ahead of Purdue, Michigan vs. Ohio State feels unusually trivial and bleak this season, and South Carolina-Clemson is just a meaningless referendum on Dabo Swinney you didn't need or ask for.

In other news, the NCAA is running a test on the 24-team playoff on Sunday with the announcement of the FCS playoff bracket, which is to say the Dakotas/Montanas Range War. The FCS champion in 12 of the past 15 years has been absorbed by those FBS ghouls, and since most of those champions have been North Dakota State (now an FBS operation; they won 10 of those titles), South Dakota State, and most recently Montana State, it seems safe to say the FCS trophy route runs roughly in parallel to I-90. But that's tomorrow's apocalypse. Saturday's opening round includes Harvard at Monmouth at noon ET, Idaho State at North Dakota at 1 p.m., and Incarnate Word at Montana at 8 p.m. The first two are on ESPN+, and UIW-Montana is on ESPNU, which is good news for you small-school psychos.

items.title: Aaron Rodgers Nukes Mike McCarthy, Then His Own Career
items.author: Samer Kalaf
items.content:
To provide further detail on the Pittsburgh Steelers' late-night benching of Aaron Rodgers, the quarterback himself appeared on Wednesday's edition of . Essentially, Rodgers said that he would never play for the team again, and he described head coach Mike McCarthy as inattentive, sleepy, and "unhealthy." In response to this TV appearance, the team has waived Rodgers.

The Steelers' benching of Rodgers came after his dismal performance in Sunday's 19-16 loss to the Philadelphia Eagles, and there's some logic behind it for purely football reasons. But the way the news was delivered was the strange part: Tuesday at 11 p.m. ET, through a team spokesperson. At the time, it wasn't even clear if Rodgers himself knew he was being benched for the team's game this Friday against Denver.

items.title: This Thanksgiving, I Hope Someone Gets You Cookies
items.author: Drew Magary
items.content:
Drew Magary’s Thursday Afternoon NFL Dick Joke Jamboroo runs every Thursday at Defector during the NFL season (except when there's a game on a Wednesday). Got something you wanna contribute? . You can also read Drew over at

It’s the holiday season in Chicago, and I am six years old. My grandma Neenie is staying at her apartment in the Streeterville neighborhood of the city, just south of the John Hancock building. Neenie and Grandpa spend the bulk of the time living down in Palm Beach, Fla., but they’ve kept the Chicago apartment because this is where they raised my mother and her three siblings, and because my family lives there now, in an apartment farther uptown. I love it when Neenie and Grandpa visit, because I know that Neenie will take me to Water Tower Place and buy me shit.

Water Tower Place is located just a few blocks away from my grandparents’ apartment, on the tony stretch of Michigan Avenue and right next to the old Chicago Avenue Pumping Station, after which the mall is named. You enter Water Tower Place from the ground floor, and then ride up into the mall alongside a series of little waterfalls cascading down between the twin escalators. I’m a grade-schooler, so I’m already predisposed to loving a good escalator ride. The fact that this one has waterfalls makes it, in my innocent mind, the most magical escalator in the world. Like riding up to heaven, if heaven had a McDonald’s in it.

items.title: San José State President Enlisted Harry Edwards To Sabotage Students’ Pro-Palestine Encampment
items.author: Samer Kalaf
items.content:
As heartening as it was to see the wave of student-led Gaza solidarity encampments across college campuses in the spring of 2024, it was just as appalling to see the crackdowns from those same schools' administrations. Across the world, university leaders showed that they were willing to sacrifice the safety of their own students and faculty, rather than divest from any companies that had financial ties to a state committing active genocide.

The most closely covered protest was at Columbia University, where the schoolultimately sent in the NYPD to dismantle the camp and assault students. The response dragged on for months; a WhatsApp group strategized on how to get the protestors deported, and put together a list of targets. Columbia graduate Mahmoud Khalil is currently appealing a deportation order, after he was held in ICE detention without criminal charges for over 100 days. On the other side of the country in 2024, UCLA's security and local police stood by as masked goons attacked students within the Gaza solidarity encampment, and tossed fireworks at them. Roughly 30 of the students and faculty attacked have sued UCLA for civil rights violations.

Because of reporting last week from Bradford William Davis and Kaya Henkes-Power at the publication Eyeblack, another school administration's grimy efforts have come to light, two years later. When San José State University students put together their Gaza solidarity encampment in 2024, they convened at the statue, a monument on campus honoring the school's alumni Tommie Smith and John Carlos for their raised fists at the 1968 Summer Olympics. The statue was created in 2005 by the Portuguese artist Ricardo Gouveia, who goes by the moniker Rigo 23.

items.title: Hark! Royal Gossip Approaches!
items.author: Jae Towle Vieira
items.content:
Have you ever wondered what a pack of specially trained bloodhounds might do for your personality? Ever considered the societal benefits of locking up your enemies in the Tower of London? Would a special dispensation from the Pope smooth things out for your most fraught marriage prospects? Could you deal with being hot enough to change the course of humanity? 

Prepare yourselves for the majesty of ! Rachelle Hampton and the team are back with a new miniseries that dares to ask the question: What is history if not gossip? Over the course of four episodes, we’ll explore the most sordid tales from one of the most charmed and chaotic periods in English history: The Wars of the Roses. Oh, and did we mention we’ll have royalty? In each episode of , Rachelle will be joined by our dowager queen Kelsey McKinney!

items.title: ‘Paper Tiger’ Is A Thrilling Homecoming For James Gray
items.author: Robert Rubsam
items.content:
Americans are forever returning to their origins, because we are always beginning again. At the start of the 20th century, three-fourths of my ancestors were still in Europe; my mother’s parents did not come over until the end of the second World War. To think of all the accidents and contingencies that brought me here, to this laptop in this café writing about the latest film by James Gray, is enough to trigger vertigo in anyone. Where does my story start? With my birth, or when my parents met on an airplane, or when my dad’s grandparents met as new immigrants in Queens? Is it only beginning now, as I type these words? Has it even begun yet?

I think Gray might understand. A director of New York City crime sagas and classically toned period pieces, his films probe the intimate in search of the mythic, and frequently achieve a kind of outer-borough biblicality. , his latest and quite possibly his best, is a story of shifting loyalties inside a Queens family called the Pearls. Irwin (Miles Teller) is an engineer, a “facts and figures” guy with a moderately successful small business, a house in Fresh Meadows, and a sea of expenses rising all around him. His wife Hester (Scarlett Johansson) wants to move to suburban Great Neck; his sons need tuition for private school and the Ivy League stamp that Irwin believes will vault them out of the ethnic middle class, and allow them to achieve what their Pratt-educated father never could. 

Over Labor Day weekend of 1986, the Pearls are visited by Irwin’s brother, Gary (Adam Driver), a recently divorced ex-cop with shiny suits, a sports car, and seemingly liquid cash flow. Swooping into their two-story brick home with a steak meal hand-delivered from Peter Luger, he wants to cut Irwin in on a lucrative opportunity, joining their security and engineering knowledge to consult on the clean-up of the outlandishly polluted Gowanus Canal. New York is changing, the Italian mob is in decline, and the canal’s new landowners are all Russian Jews like the Pearls, though of more recent vintage. “Communism’s over,” Gary explains. “Everyone wants their piece of the pie.”

items.title: A ‘Distraction’ Reunion On ‘All Ball’, Just For You
items.author: Drew Magary
items.content:
The NFL’s Thanksgiving weekend slate starts tonight, with the wholly manufactured “Thanksgiving Eve” game on Netflix. This slate features a ton of juicy matchups, almost as recompense for the previous two weeks of dreadful games that you and I have had to endure. Every one of the five-throwgasm showdowns spread out across the next six days(!) merits thorough analysis. Alas, because my co-host Arif Hasan was on the road all day yesterday, you the audience get David Roth instead.

My old co-host is versed in football, so don’t be alarmed. You’ll still get plenty of chitchat about the games at hand. But Roth and I also carve out some time to marvel at the election results, to ask big-picture questions about the league’s desire to occupy every available time slot, and to discuss Portuguese egg tarts. Truly, a feast for the ears. As always, we do NOT talk about gambling or fantasy football. Roth tried to get in a brief fantasy note, but I quickly shut that talk down and had my friend summarily killed after we’d recorded this episode. Didn’t want to do it; felt I it to him.

items.title: It’s Never Too Late To Be The Best Band In The World Again
items.author: Drew Magary
items.content:
We begin at Webster Hall in New York City. I'm standing on the main floor with the rest of the general admission patrons. My best friend Howard is with me. He's been waiting nearly as many years as I have for what's about to transpire. So has everyone else in the room. Many of them are already drunk. Many more are still queued up in the line at the merch stand, which has run out of at least one line of T-shirts and will likely run out of others.

Howard and I are soaking in the pre-concert playlist playing over the loudspeakers, and waiting for the lights to go dark. I've put in my earplugs. I can't hear anything Howard says, but it doesn't matter. He's ready. I'm ready. Everyone is ready, because we're about to witness the resurrection of Sugar, one of the greatest bands of the 1990s. None of us believed this band would reunite. Never considered the possibility, really. Shit, prior to tonight I didn't even think the members of Sugar—guitarist/vocalist Bob Mould, bassist David Barbe, drummer Malcolm Travis—had considered the idea themselves. For Mould, the ringleader, Sugar wasn't even the most famous band he'd played in. The fact that they're here together on this opening night of the "Love You Even Still" tour, and that we're all here to witness it, feels like a happy fluke.

But this is no fluke at all. This is a reunion that required many years, plus a well-timed video birthday card, to become a reality. I have seen Mould on his own in concert more times than I can count, but I've never seen him take the stage live with Travis and Barbe. That's because I discovered Sugar's music a beat too late. They had already broken up before my roommate put on their second album, File Under: Easy Listening, in our college dorm room. Once I heard the opening chords to "Gee Angel," I knew right away that Sugar was my band. That they would be my band. If I never got to see them in the flesh, so be it. The music had me forever. I knew it back in 1997, and I still know it today, 29 years later.

items.title: Aaron Rodgers Benched For First And Possibly Final Time
items.author: Barry Petchesky
items.content:
Aaron Rodgers will not start the Pittsburgh Steelers' next game, the team announced late Tuesday night. Curiously late, actually, and in a manner that reeks of intrigue. Nothing Rodgers does is normal, so why should the potential end of his NFL career be?

Mike McCarthy was unequivocal about it on Monday: "Aaron Rodgers is our quarterback," he said, when asked about making a change one day after a loss to the Eagles that featured Rodgers putting up one of the feeblest halves of QB play in 20 years. Something must have changed, and quickly. "After a series of meetings," as Adam Schefter put it, "'some good, some bad,'" the call was made. It "was a coach's decision," ESPN reports. At 11:10 p.m. Tuesday, an odd time for an announcement, the Steelers put out a statement from a team spokesperson, an odd source for a personnel decision, that Rodgers will be in street clothes for Friday's game.

items.title: Michigan Pulls Offer On Incoming Athletic Director, Still Owes Him Money
items.author: Ray Ratto
items.content:
The Protect College Sports Act is a bad idea that seems stalled in Congress, and now we're finding out that the things most endangering college sports are coming from inside the house. In this case, the house in question is in Ann Arbor, Michigan, where ESPN's Pete Thamel reported that Trev Alberts, who was hired last week as the University of Michigan's athletic director, has now been un-hired for that role.

Yes, Alberts has apparently been fired before being hired as the Michigan AD, which may not quite be unprecedented but is inarguably damned weird. What made Michigan reverse course was that Alberts was the AD at Nebraska when Ashley Scoggin, a women's basketball player, sued the school in 2024 after being kicked off the team because of an alleged sexual relationship with assistant coach Chuck Love. Alberts was specifically named in the lawsuit for supporting the head coach's decision, not adequately addressing the assistant's misconduct, and, in a meeting with Scoggin's parents, supporting the decision to kick Scoggin off the team for dishonesty rather than dealing with the allegation of Love's misconduct. Alberts has denied those allegations in a court filing opposing the suit, but the baggage he would have brought to his new job, so soon after Michigan's issues with former football coach Sherrone Moore, seems to have given the school's administrators enough pause to bail on Alberts.

The sidebar here is that Alberts already signed a memorandum of understanding that he would be paid $17.2 million over the next five years. According to ESPN, Alberts' lawyer Tom Mars claimed that Alberts, who pronounced himself "shocked and disheartened" at the news, has not been given a reason for the school pulling out. Mars also maintained that there was no reference in the MOU to a background check. In other words, the fight isn't over the job but the money. Nothing says college sports quite like that last sentence.

items.title: Solving The Olivia Rodrigo–Taylor Swift Songwriting Credit Debate Once And For All
items.author: Patrick Redford
items.content:
All of pop music can be thought of as existing on a temporal and stylistic continuum. Every up-and-coming artist is influenced to make music by the people they grew up listening to, and the truest marker of success is making music that's beloved enough to influence the next generation of musicians. In one sense, this is a straightforward description of the passage of time, but it's also the foundation of a complicated, fascinating legal space, where something like a particular yell can be thought of as proprietary.

Which is all to say, I find the Taylor Swift–Olivia Rodrigo songwriting credit debate, the subject of this week's episode of , extremely fascinating. Three songs on Rodrigo's 2021 debut album , all of which was written by Rodrigo and her collaborator Dan Nigro, were the subjects of post-facto songwriting credit adjustments. Swift and her collaborators are now listed as the writers of two tracks, while two members of Paramore are listed as writers on one, despite none of them actually writing any of the material. How did something that strange happen? What does it say about the way intellectual property functions in music? Can someone own elements of a song?

We got into all that and more with the great Nate Sloan and Charlie Harding of . This week's episode is the first in a three-episode, season-ending mini arc that we are calling Who Owns An Idea? The next episode is about IP theft in fashion, while the season finale is about AI.

items.title: Unmasking The International Man Of Mystery And Nets Twitter, With James Herbert And Ock Sportello
items.author: Patrick Redford
items.content: This week's episode of marks the second straight week of interviewing the author of a landmark piece of sportswriting. This time, we were joined by James Herbert, who wrote a profile of longtime NBC investigative reporter and prolific NetsDaily blogger Bob Windrem for The Ringer, as well as longtime favorite Ock Sportello, Nets fan and NetsDaily scholar. The descriptors "NBC investigative reporter" and "prolific NetsDaily blogger" both undersell Windrem. He was the first reporter to learn of Al Qaeda's role in 9/11; spent decades breaking extremely important, thorny international news stories; and also possesses perhaps the greatest corpus of knowledge on Nets of minor import, such as Sundiata Gaines, Cui Yongxi, and Milton Doyle. We spent a long time digging into the story.

items.title: Jayden Daniels Has The Juice Again
items.author: Lauren Theisen
items.content:
With under a minute to go, it looked like Washington had let the game slip through their fingers. The Cincinnati Bengals were behind 19-17 late, but they quickly got into kicking range. On second down, however, Joe Burrow lofted a pass right over the middle, and Commanders DB Rasul Douglas was in perfect position to make a clutch interception. Instead, the ball bounced off his hand, twice. To make matters worse, Douglas laid face-down on the ground in frustration after the near-pick, and the officials charged Washington with an injury timeout, their final one. They couldn't stop the clock after their third-down sack, which meant Evan McPherson's go-ahead kick passed through the uprights with only 46 seconds remaining.

That was all the time that Jayden Daniels needed. Coming off a game where he threw the winning touchdown in the final minute, the Commanders QB took advantage of a prevent defense to complete two long passes over the middle, setting up Drew Stevens for the winning 26-yard kick. For the first time since the 2024 playoffs, Washington has won back-to-back games.

items.title: NWSL Players Association Has Concerns About Bay FC’s Treatment Of Players Who Have Taken Maternity Leave
items.author: Abigail Segel
items.content:
The NWSL Players Association is concerned that Bay FC violated two different sections of the league’s collective bargaining agreement related to parental rights, according to PA Executive Director Meghann Burke. One of the sections is about non-discrimination, and one is about parental leave in the case that it overlaps with an expiring contract. The union is evaluating if there is enough information to file a grievance.

On Nov. 13, Bay announced its end-of-season roster updates. Three players who are new mothers—Caprice Dydasco, Abby Dahlkemper, and Emily Menges—were out of contract with the club and would not be re-signed. 

“On its face, we’re concerned there were three moms under contract with Bay who gave birth and were on maternity leave, and none of them are returning next season,” Burke told Defector. “Right away, that sort of raises an index of suspicion, where you try and understand what’s going on.”

items.title: It’s Josh Johnson Time In The NFL
items.author: Ray Ratto
items.content:
He's back! He's back, he's back, he's freaking BACK! The Josh Johnson's Race Against Time Netflix series is surely just around the corner, and all Johnson needs to get it over is land one more gig before retirement so that he can become the first player to play for half the teams in his chosen sport.

We have visited the topic of Johnson's peripatetic journey through professional football before, with our first celebration dating all the way back to the dying embers of the COVID era. Johnson has come and gone as needed and as usual since, and the only reason to re-dredge this particular part of the bay is that Johnson started and finished Sunday's Arizona Cardinals game at Kansas City. It went about the way it should; the Cardinals are punting the season, and got punted in turn by the Chiefs, 34-7. Nobody seemed overly troubled by either the game play or the ensuing numbers, because nobody was under the illusion that this was an especially meaningful game.

That very much includes the Cardinals. They are uniquely awful because they are ritually awful; having to start four quarterbacks in four weeks is some deeply and unmistakably Cardinals Stuff. That they have reached the Josh Johnson stage of their season this early is fairly Cardinals as well, but less novel. There, at least, they have plenty of company.

items.title: Jensen Huang Returns To Nvidia After Mr. Market Deems Him Too Indispensable
items.author: Patrick Redford
items.content:
Two weeks after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was forced to admit to having conducted one of his many multiply illicit affairs with a woman accused of working as a spy for the Chinese government, 11 days after he was forced out of his position at the titanic chipmaker and tentpole of the world economy, and one week after I made a pilgrimage to the holy site in Silicon Valley where he came up with the idea for the multi-trillion dollar company, Jensen Huang is back. The Nvidia board announced on Monday morning that he would return to his position, reassuring the public and Nvidia investors that Huang's "reinstatement poses no national security risk."

Momentum had been building toward Huang's reinstatement since he was forced out. The strongest push reportedly has come from within Nvidia, which might seem somewhat surprising, given reports of Huang having "terrorized" and "humiliated" staffers who annoyed him or otherwise got in his way. Concerning as those reports may be, they don't really matter when considered against the credit Huang popularly receives for how much money Nvidia has made for everyone. The myth of the lone visionary CEO is largely a marketing fiction, but in the case of Nvidia, which has flirted with a $5 trillion market cap, it's more or less true. Huang created a corporate architecture that gave him an unusual amount of power, and he used it to make a series of risky and ultimately very successful bets. This is why so many current and former Nvidia people called on the board to Stand With Jensen.

As for the people opposed to Huang's return, some of them are AI people who find themselves on the opposite side of Huang in the debate over closed vs. open models. Huang has long argued for AI development that favors open-source–style knowledge sharing over the closed-off frontier lab model, a stance that makes sense, given that the open model of development creates the largest and hungriest possible market for his company's chips. The frontier lab model's argument against this mode is that the political-religious stakes in the race to create the machine god before everybody else are just too high to allow for anything as squishy as sharing; as with Huang's case, that argument neatly aligns with their business interests.

items.title: A Shooting Slump Spells Celtic Doom
items.author: Giri Nathan
items.content:
The Boston Celtics opened the season 11-2, and everything looked green and healthy. Jayson Tatum slid back back into his perpetual "No. 4 in MVP voting" status, newly added Paul George was hooping as if de-aged, and head coach Joe Mazzulla's offensive philosophy looked unimpeachable (despite having often invited impeachment in postseasons past). Put the defense in rotation, find an open three, and the math will carry you to victory. Through those first 13 games, it really did. The Celtics were throwing up 43 threes a game (fifth-most in the league) and making them at 38.5 percent clip (fourth-best in the league). They looked cleaner and sharper than they did in last year's Jaylen Brown-led campaign, an even purer distillation of Mazzulla ball.

Maybe that should have prepared fans to confront an even purer dark side of Mazzulla ball, too. Since then, the Celtics have screeched into a four-game skid: hosting the Orlando Magic, then losing on the road to the Denver Nuggets, Sacramento Kings, and Golden State Warriors by 10 points, 4 points, 1 point, and 1 point, respectively. That's cause for alarm, given that this team hasn't lost four games in a row since May 2021. Sunday's 88-87 loss to a Warriors team led in scoring by Brandin Podziemski, Gui Santos, and Charles Bassey was particularly gruesome. The Celtics led for most of the second half, but still went on to lose the game, despite the Warriors failing to score a point in the final two minutes and 30 seconds of regulation. Tatum was 0-of-7 in the second half, including an attempted game-winner over Draymond Green from the elbow.

items.title: Tarik Skubal’s Huge Mets Deal May Be The Last Of Its Kind
items.author: Kathryn Xu
items.content:
Hey, at least it wasn't the Dodgers. It was, however, the other, generally less frightening team you might have expected: Jon Heyman reported Sunday afternoon that Tarik Skubal would be signing with the New York Mets. ESPN's Jeff Passan followed up to say that Skubal's contract will be worth $450 million over nine years, rocketing past Yoshinobu Yamamoto's 12-year, $325 million contract for the most expensive pitching contract in MLB history by total value.

The best comparison for Skubal is not Yamamoto but Gerrit Cole, who signed a nine-year, $324 million contract with the New York Yankees back in 2019, which, with some very hasty back-of-the-napkin inflation math, was worth around the same value as Skubal's contract today. At the time that Cole signed the contract, he was 29, a year younger than Skubal now, and though he had yet to win a Cy Young at that point in his career, Cole ranked in the top five in voting in each of the previous two years. With two years now remaining on Cole's contract, reasonable and unreasonable Yankees fans alike would mostly agree that even after he lost a year and change to Tommy John surgery, the sum total of Cole's contract will turn out to have been worth it: the 2023 Cy Young award, solid postseason starts, likely no truly unplayable years through the end of his contract, and spanning enough time for the Yankees' beard rule to be repealed while he was still with the team.

If Skubal's contract plays out as well as Cole's, even Tommy John–inclusive and beard rule–exclusive, then by heuristic, it will have been a successful contract for the Mets. There are more obvious confounding factors for Skubal than there were at the time of Cole's contract: Skubal is a year older and, earlier this season, missed time to remove a "loose body" from his elbow. Ideally a starting pitcher would have all their bodies fixed in place; some number of those bodies being loose amounts to a negative indicator for long-term health. And while Cole's first season with the Yankees was shortened due to a global pandemic that nobody could have predicted when he signed on Dec. 18, 2019, Skubal's contract comes just over a week before baseball's collective bargaining agreement will expire; it is increasingly unlikely, as owners continue pushing for a salary cap and floor and a lockout appears ever more inevitable, that Skubal's first season will be a complete one.

items.title: Max Verstappen Couldn’t Pass Up A Chance To Bully George Russell
items.author: Luis Paez-Pumar
items.content:
While both the Drivers' and Constructors' Championships are done and dusted in the 2026 Formula 1 season—the former thanks to almost-child Kimi Antonelli's majestic season, and the latter also thanks to his Mercedes teammate George Russell—there are still important storylines to be sorted out, which now include the continuation of F1's most compelling psychodrama, featuring Russell and Max Verstappen.

Late on Saturday night, Verstappen did what he has done in all but one of the Las Vegas Grand Prix races since it debuted in 2023: He won. Verstappen is now 3-for-4 on the Strip, only losing out in 2024 to, of all people, Russell. That part isn't particularly relevant, but it's a fun quirk to this rivalry that has become heated once more. During free practice on Friday, Verstappen overtook Russell ahead of a push lap, and when Russell tried to take the position back on the inside, the pair collided, essentially ruining that practice lap for both.

This infuriated Russell, who said that while "there's nothing in the rules to say that you cannot overtake someone who is starting their lap," a move like Verstappen's can screw over the other driver. He went on to say that Verstappen does this all the time, to a lot of drivers, and that he's had enough of it. "Everybody accepts it, and I am not just going to accept somebody to screw me over like this, and walk around like they are bigger and better than everyone else. Somebody has got to stand up to that guy."

items.title: Dylan Larkin Déménage À Montréal
items.author: Lauren Theisen
items.content:
After an agonizingly long trade-demand/suspension saga that featured the former Red Wings captain fully abandoning his team a month into this season, Dylan Larkin has received his wish—mostly. As one of Kash Patel's good buddies, the disgruntled Detroiter was reportedly wielding his no-movement clause to keep the Wings from resolving his situation with a Canadian team. But a few weeks without playing hockey (or getting paid) apparently softened his stance. Larkin will be suiting up for the division rival Montreal Canadiens, and in return, Wings interim GM Shawn Horcoff got a bushel of draft picks, a backup goalie at best in Sam Montembeault, a draft-bust depth forward in Kirby Dach, and a real prospect in Michael Hage.

If it feels like the Habs won this trade, it's because they gave up zero good NHL players for four-and-a-half reasonably priced years of a guy who should serve as a really great second-line center on a contender. Montreal is already pretty busy with nifty young forwards, but the 30-year-old Larkin should slot in nicely thanks to his two-way talents and goalscoring pedigree. Playing on by far the most stacked team that's ever employed him, he won't be the focal point that he was in Detroit, but it shouldn't be hard for him to find a place in the hearts of fans who were chanting "We want Larkin!" the last time he visited.

So far this season, at 14-6-4, the Canadiens sit comfortably in playoff position but are in no state to refuse more help. Their young superstars, plus the tier below, are producing less than they were when they set a torrid pace last year, while goaltender Jakub Dobes, coming off a strong rookie campaign, now backs up the even-younger Jacob Fowler. I'm looking at the 22-year-old winger Juraj Slafkovsky (two goals, after 30 last year) as the guy who stands to benefit most from having Larkin as his center. But his arrival should be appreciated by everyone from Cole Caufield and Nick Suzuki on offense to Noah Dobson on defense, because he'll make each individual load a little lighter. Montreal is counting on its core to produce the franchise's first Stanley Cup since 1993, and the current cast will have at minimum four shots at it, with a decent amount of cap space to add even more weapons.

items.title: Brock Purdy Made The Vikings Go Bust
items.author: Tom Ley
items.content:
The NFL season presents few things as satisfying as a game that promises to answer questions: Is this team really a contender?Is that guy really an MVP candidate? Does that scheme actually work against good teams? These are a few of the questions that swirled around Sunday night's matchup between the Minnesota Vikings and San Francisco 49ers, who came into the game as two of the NFC's best teams, but left the Niners' 35-10 victory as something else.

Success against the Vikings depends on one's ability to deal with pressure, and not the metaphorical kind. Brian Flores's defense blitzes at a historically high rate, and in the process of becoming the league's most fearsome defense has raised some interesting philosophical questions about NFL schemes. Should teams just blitz on every down? If not, why hasn't any team punished the Vikings for doing essentially that?

Every blitz is a bet that the defense will reach and disrupt the quarterback before he has time to find an open receiver in the vacated space, and it's one that Flores has been winning more often than not. Every gambler with that kind of success rate has an edge, and Flores's seems to be his understanding that, in the aggregate, there just aren't enough good quarterbacks and functional offenses in the league to punish his aggressiveness. Think about how much bad quarterback play happens every Sunday, and ask yourself why any defensive coordinator should hesitate to turn up the pressure on offenses that already struggle with the basics.

items.title: Kansas City Broke Through The Noise
items.author: Abigail Segel
items.content:
Kansas City wanted blood. Knowing the Washington Spirit would look to dazzle home fans with pretty football, and knowing those fans—desperate for a championship after two consecutive final defeats—would be loud and temperamental, the Current set out to disrupt, disrupt, disrupt. 

Laney Rouse, the Current’s only starting rookie, took the first kill. Washington was coming off an early attacking sequence when the ball bounced over toward the sideline. Trinity Rodman set herself up for the trap, but Rouse had already gathered her momentum and crashed into Rodman’s back like a wrecking ball. The face of the Washington Spirit tumbled, hard. Rouse got away without seeing a card, and the home fans were apoplectic. Rodman didn’t get up for minutes. 

Rodman’s health was key to the Spirit’s success this year. In 2025, she missed months while struggling with a back injury and only appeared for 35 total minutes in the postseason. But after an offseason in which she chose Washington and the power of her stardom changed the league itself, she found her groove. A deserving MVP nominee, Rodman notched 13 goals and eight assists in the regular season and didn’t miss a match. The sight of Rodman floundering about on the ground was nightmarish for fans at Audi Field.

items.title: Are The Knicks Back?
items.author: Rachelle Hampton
items.content:
Within the first three minutes of playing time in Saturday night’s game against the Portland Trail Blazers, I found myself wondering (and maybe even hoping): Are the Knicks back? 

My suspicions had started to rise only sometime in the last week, somewhere between the reigning champs' back-to-back victories against the Raptors and their hard-fought win against the Timberwolves. It was in the second game against the Raptors that I started to see glimmers of what could make this current New York roster so magical to watch; that was the same game where Karl-Anthony Towns declared that his team, after a sleepy start to the season, was finally playing “like the Knicks again … with that physicality and that energy that made us so special last year.”

So when I saw that KAT, one of the few bright spots of consistency in this season so far, along with the steadfast, laconic OG Anunoby, were both out for Saturday night’s game against Portland, my first thought was lol, we’re 100 percent going to lose. Then I saw that Deni Avdija was cleared to return to the Blazers after missing the last two games, and I thought, Oh, so we’re 1,000 percent going to lose. Even without Avdija, the Blazers had been surprisingly competitive, led offensively by a newly returned Damian Lillard.

items.title: Oh No, I Can’t Stop Watching People Play ‘GTA VI’
items.author: Brandy Jensen
items.content:
I did not imagine that the release of would have any meaningful impact on my life, for the simple reason that I am not a gamer. I know and even respect a few people for whom video games are important, but I mainly regard this in the same way I do friends who really like square dancing, or go to church: nice for them, but not really my business.

While I have, in the past, dated gamers and even come to occasionally enjoy watching them play video games, that was mainly because I'm bossy and liked telling them , or Open that box, I bet there's something inside. Backseat driving a video game can be fun, but only insofar as I can manipulate what's happening. The appeal of Twitch, where you are simply one of dozens or hundreds of spectators watching someone else play a game, has always been totally, utterly alien to me. This would be true even without the dangers of encountering slurs in a chat or being confronted by the ever-present sight of anything that could be reasonably called "a gaming rig." No thank you.

And yet, I have found my conviction wavering recently as I find myself strangely compelled to click on clip after clip of people playing . It started innocently enough, as people kept insisting that this game was teaching men to be thoughtful partners. I watched clips of people doing things Lucia will appreciate: buying groceries, taking her shopping, picking up flowers. I watched a guy make thoughtful decisions about how she might like to wear her hair. Soon I'd moved on to following along as people make Jason lovingly turn their house into a home, or invite Lucia to take the driver's seat on an aquatic adventure.

items.title: Blackpool To Coach: Happy Birthday, You’re Fired
items.author: Ray Ratto
items.content:
Much derision fell upon the people who run Blackpool Football Club of League One, the third tier of English football, when it wished head coach Ian Evatt a happy birthday seven hours before firing him on Thursday. It did seem exceedingly cruel, even by the prevailing bastardy standards of our time.

Then again, only a simp would believe that human decency enters into decisions like these. Your holidays aren't anyone else's, so stop acting like they are. This is especially true when the only thing keeping you out of a relegation spot is goal differential. In that situation, your employer very well might call you "Gaffer" in the morning and can you by happy hour. That's the gig.

The rudimentarily funny part is how the club announced his firing. According to them, Evatt "departed his role," as though he chose to fire himself. This is not just an English politeness thing, either. Teams and the media types who exist to disseminate their team sources' text messages love to describe firings as "a parting of ways," or the coach "leaving his role," or beating feet "by mutual agreement," and over time, that creeps into the language used by normal fans. It's as if we each have an HR goblin in our homes, ready to spring malevolently into action at any moment.

items.title: Jessica Berman Still Doesn’t Have Very Clear Answers
items.author: Lesley Ryder
items.content:
— Thrice a year, the media gets the chance to speak with NWSL commissioner Jessica Berman. And as the league has grown, so have the pomp and circumstance around the event. For this year’s edition, famed soccer announcer Andrés Cantor introduced the commissioner to the stage.  

Many questions were asked of Berman, and very few of them—especially the thornier ones—were really answered.

Berman’s speech glided through the NWSL’s wins in attendance and viewership, and she shared lofty goals for the years ahead while also giving opaque answers (or sometimes complete non-answers) on issues like field quality, anti-trans activists coming to games, and one team possibly relocating. Each answer sounded like it was crafted from the same girl-boss leadership academy that produced outgoing WNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert.

items.title: Fiona The Hippo Lived And Died In The Spotlight
items.author: Sabrina Imbler
items.content:
It was, it seems, a freak accident. Around two weeks ago, a child standing by Hippo Cove at the Cincinnati Zoo tossed a knit cap into the air, which was caught by a whirling ceiling fan and launched through the one-foot gap between the 12-foot-tall viewing window and the ceiling, where it landed in the enclosure's pool. Because Nile hippos can grow to be 3,000 pounds, zookeepers and veterinarians are not allowed to share space. There must be a protective barrier between the hippos and the humans, which prevented the swift removal of the hat. This is how Fiona the celebrity hippopotamus ate the hat that would kill her.

After Fiona ate the hat, veterinarians started monitoring the hippo's progress in passing the object. They took her off exhibit. They offered her treats to encourage digestion. They gave her fluids and an enema and a colonoscopy with a nine-foot scope. They placed her atop a vibration plate used to rehabilitate horses, hoping the vibrations might spur some movement in her digestive tract. On Nov. 17, an ultrasound showed her intestines were bunching. Hippos have multi-chambered stomachs that help them digest plants, and these chambers made the hat impossible to see or retrieve with an endoscope. Surgery was out of the question. The keepers didn't even know where the hat was located inside Fiona—her stomach, intestine, or colon—or if it had unraveled. Hippo skin can be over two inches thick, making it difficult for vets to access veins for anesthesia or close incisions. Hippos also need access to water, and Fiona would have needed to be out of the water for several days for her incisions to heal. Despite the veterinarians' best efforts and an outpouring of goodwill from Fiona's countless fans, the hippo died on Nov. 19 at the tender age of 9. "Our animal care team was heroic in their efforts to save her," zoo director Dave Jenike said in a statement. "They did everything possible, but her body couldn’t fight anymore."

Fiona was the first celebrity hippo of our age. This superlative sounds silly, and also it is true. Without Fiona, there might be no Moo Deng. The Thai hippo would exist, but she might never have been a star without the Ohioan who paved the way for boisterous hippo calves whose big personalities outshone their still-considerable heft. Fiona made headlines before she was born—her fetal image was captured in the first-ever ultrasound of a Nile hippo's womb—and she became a global star soon after she was born in January 2017, six weeks premature. She was just 29 pounds (the normal range for Nile hippo calves is 55 to 120 pounds) and she could not stand up to nurse from her mother, Bibi. The keepers managed to collect Bibi's milk to bottle-feed Fiona, along with other supplements, and cared for the baby around the clock. Things were touch and go. At three weeks, Fiona was not drinking, and a Cincinnati nurse managed to find a vein via ultrasound to give the baby a life-saving IV.

items.title: ‘Madden’ Makes One Of The NFL’s Biggest Characters Feel Silly And Small
items.author: Ray Ratto
items.content:
Al Davis's afterlife is difficult enough to imagine under any circumstances, but it takes an exceptionally grisly imagination to make him a character in a Hallmark movie written in an hour by a seventh grader.

And to add imaginary insult to conceptual injury, Davis has been made into a  in a Hallmark movie written in an hour by a seventh grader. The actual film is not made by Hallmark, where superficiality is raised to raison d'etre and plotting and dialogue are upstaged by tinsel and presents strewn about the town gazebo, but by Amazon. Less explicably, it is co-written and directed by David O. Russell, and not a middle schooler on a deadline. It is called  and is about John Madden, mostly, and most of what Christian Bale does as Al Davis amounts to reacting to things that Nicolas Cage, as John Madden, does. It's a romcom without the rom and precious little com. Now that's making hell relatable to us all.

As you may have already heard,  is galactically bad. It's a movie about a man far too large for the biopic genre, maybe even two such men if you want to raise Davis to Madden's cultural stature, and that's its essential problem. There is a lot of competition, there, but "fundamentally should not exist" is hard to top as problems go. It's also a movie released around the holidays, when movie IQs are lowered by a good 25 points by the mere act of their being released to a national audience preparing for its own annual festive stupefaction.

items.title: Semafor Paid A Trump Goon $100,000 To Make Its Events More Evil
items.author: Albert Burneko
items.content:
It's fine not to know who Jason Miller is. There are a lot of Jasons Miller out there; when I hear the name "Jason Miller," I think of the soulful, sad-eyed actor who portrayed Fr. Damian Karras in . This blog is not about that Jason Miller. This blog is about the following much worse guy also named Jason Miller:

The above chinless goblin is one of the many guys whose life's work is orbiting around Donald Trump doing ... whatever, but mainly just existing horribly where they can interact with others of their ilk and monetize, crudely, their access to each other and, through each other, to the worst president in U.S. history. This Jason Miller served as a spokesperson for Trump's 2016 presidential campaign and, after Trump won that election, was tapped for the position of White House communications director; he left that job within days when it came to light that he'd had an extramarital affair with Trump advisor A.J. Delgado and was the deadbeat father of her child. Miller later left a job at CNN after Delgado alleged, in a lawsuit seeking child support, that he had slipped abortifacient drugs into the drink of a previous, unnamed, pregnant girlfriend; Miller sued Gizmodo Media Group and reporter Katherine Krueger for $100 million, unsuccessfully, over their having published a summary of the allegations.

items.title: Victor Wembanyama’s Blister Inspires Purely Downward Jump Shot
items.author: Giri Nathan
items.content:
The thrown-in dunk, or "thrunk" if you prefer, is no new phenomenon. Vertically gifted players have long been hurling basketballs down into the hoop from a distance, without their hands directly touching the rim. But has that hurling motion ever been replaced by the soft wrist flick of a jump shot? Have you seen a jump shot begin from above the rim?

On Thursday night, San Antonio Spurs center Victor Wembanyama developed his own variation on the thrunk, after collecting a hit-ahead pass from his teammate Stephon Castle. All alone on the other end,Wemby went up with a guide hand on the side of the ball, and with his shooting hand he flicked the ball directly down into the hoop. In the official play-by-play, it was logged as a pedestrian "running dunk," but the truth is out there. We saw the shunk.

items.title: It’s Familiar At The Top
items.author: Ray Ratto
items.content:
Last week went a long way toward revealing December and January, which sucks a bit because most of the surviving mysteries regarding conference championships, playoff berths and firings are largely being settled. The weekend highlights included Oklahoma pitching hissy fits at Ole Miss and the SEC office over uncontrollable travel issues, then winning on Sunday; Arizona State reinventing pregame prep by flying to Orlando on game day to beat UCF, 26-13; and Washington State getting its second win of the season by beating Colorado State, 73-7, with nine rushing touchdowns. Most of the remaining slate was watching the form of the last two months solidify and harden into an easily predictable future.

For all the chaos we yammer about, the same old stories are being told the same old way because college football is devoted to business as usual, plus the hiring hall at James Madison. There isn't even the manufactured drama of whether Notre Dame will get in the College Football Playoff (it will), or whether USC will (it won't). The first hints of traditional rivalry games begin this weekend, but most of them will happen right after Thanksgiving, and the matchups we do get are circumstantially tepid. Frankly, if we were you (and believe us, nobody wants that in either direction), we'd sit out this week and wait for the last conference championships to be sorted. You won't miss much. Even the possibility of UMass (remember them?) nailing down its first bowl game since joining big-kid football is effectively over, after a 34-33 loss to lowly Akron on Wednesday. That makes us all feel like right charlies for getting our hopes up to begin with.

items.title: Alex Ovechkin Is A Tough Watch These Days
items.author: Barry Petchesky
items.content:
It is becoming physically painful to watch Alexander Ovechkin play hockey. In this, his 22nd and final NHL season, all at once he has started to look his age. He hasn't been the most ... let's say skater for years now, but he had somehow found ways to defy the calendar and continue to put up 30- and 40-goal seasons. That magic has run out. With just one goal in 20 games this season, none in his last 15, the NHL's greatest scorer is in the longest goal drought of his career.

Over the last few years, Ovechkin's game has contracted to encompass only his shot. That snipe from the circle hadn't abandoned him, even as his footspeed did—he's the slowest forward in the league by both average and top skating speed. As long as he was scoring, it was easier to ignore, if still a little upsetting for anyone who remembers the freight train he was in his youth. But the shot's gone too, at least over the first quarter of the season. "Chances are there,” Ovechkin insisted Thursday night, after Washington's 6-3 home loss to Buffalo. “Sometimes you hold stick too tight."

Without the goals, what's left is a large old man, skating stiffly and slowly up and down the neutral zone, waiting for his teammates to make something happen, because he can't backcheck, and he can't go coast to coast anymore. Against the Sabres, with the game already well out of hand, he was chased down from behind on a potential 2-on-1. An unmistakable sign it's time to hit the exits.

items.title: “Mind If I Join?”
items.author: Sabrina Imbler
items.content:
The winsome fly does not appear very winsome, unless you are also a fly. The fly looks like any other of its kind, with eyes as red as goji berriesand a coat of horrible hairs. It is about the size of a housefly, and you probably would not be able to distinguish it from its more common counterpart if you saw one buzzing around your kitchen.

Fortunately for you, however, the winsome fly has no interest in you and your humble human existence. The winsome fly is a parasitoid, and it only has big red eyes for the Japanese beetle, . The Japanese beetle is the winsome fly's only known host, which explains in part why the fly above is staring so intently at the beetles. But the winsome fly has a trick up its hairy little sleeve. It has learned that the easiest way to parasitize the poor beetle is when the bug is at its most vulnerable, meaning when she is —a beetle caught in the throes of beetle passion, an insect —per a new paper recently published in .

items.title: There’s Comfort In Conquering The Past
items.author: Luis Paez-Pumar
items.content:
The first time I played was during a hurricane. It was late 1999, I was 10 years old, Hurricane Irene was bearing down on Miami, and my friend Ryan had come over to spend the night. He had brought his copy of , the game a year old at that point, and his plan was that we should play it all the way to the end. This was a bold goal for two idiot preteen boys, and though we plowed through the entire Child Link part of the game and the start of Adult Link's quest to release the temple sages, the Water Temple claimed us as its own. We didn't have a Prima strategy guide or the internet to help us out, so after hours (and I do mean hours) of raising and lowering water levels, we gave up. I didn't end up beating my own copy of , which my dad bought for me as soon as the hurricane passed, until the next summer in Venezuela, but even then, even as an idiot preteen boy, I knew I had played something special.

Twenty-seven years later, I am playing something special again. Well, I am playing the same thing, but newer, fresher, and more beautiful. I am playing the remake of , and I have loved every second of it so far. As a remake, this is a work of art. The graphics are gorgeous, if a bit shiny. The story is as good as it ever was, only now with a lot more voice acting that gives characters personality. The gameplay is much the same, albeit with some quality-of-life changes; the ability to swap equipped items with one button is a huge upgrade to pausing and going into the menu every three seconds. I'm not saying that the remake is now the best way to play —there's something to be said for the friction that came with the original's technical limitations—but I saying that the remake justifies its own existence with an attention to detail and a commitment to thrilling gameplay that shines through in every second of playtime.

items.title: The Katseye Concussion Saga Raises The Question Of Who’s In Charge In K-Pop
items.author: Alex Sujong Laughlin
items.content:
Last week, I couldn’t stop watching videos of Katseye's performance in Austin, Texas, where three members of the group writhed on stage while a fourth, Megan Skiendiel—who had recently suffered a concussion—wore protective sunglasses and was propped up on a stool to the side. She sat with her legs crossed, expressionless, as if she were not on stage under flashing lights but instead waiting for her name to be called at the DMV. Mere feet away, her comrades in ass-shaking executed their choreography with their usual precision.

Skiendiel’s presence on stage adds so little to the performance that you wonder why she’s even there. Every once in a while, she raised her mic to sing her part in a song, devoid of any expression or movement. The dissonance of the scene was so absurd that it generated memesofitsown, and even fan art; this week, Skiendiel posted backstage photos of herself in her sunglasses, with the caption “Cuntcussion.”

items.title: Is ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ What The Music Business Needed Most?
items.author: Israel Daramola
items.content:
, a column where I share the music and musical topics I’ve been fixated on recently.

The music business is in trouble. Everybody keeps telling me about it, so it must be true, right? And it especially must be true of rap, which is totally, definitelydying, and actually already dead, and the worst it has ever been, according to several people who own microphones and audio/video recording equipment and exclusively upload to YouTube. All right, sure. I mean, it's not like there aren't troubling indicators out there, so maybe everybody is right: about music, about rap, about the business.

items.title: The NFL Trade Deadline Is Fine Right Where It Is
items.author: Drew Magary
items.content:
If you were up early last Sunday, you may have borne witness to this NFL season’s most catastrophic play, in which Detroit Lions edge rusher Aidan Hutchinson took out Pats QB Drake Maye for the season, and then took out for the season mere seconds later. ACH!

Not only did these two injuries severely hamper the postseason prospects of both the Patriots and Lions, but they also turned what would have otherwise been a compelling Munich game into a big ol’ doo-doo fest. Even worse, both Detroit and New England suffered these losses the NFL’s trade deadline had already passed. If the Pats want help at QB, they’re gonna have to make nice with Handsome Jimmy Garoppolo, or grab some other slob off the free-agent wire. And if the Lions want to reinforce their pass rush … well, they can’t. They’re just gonna have to score 60 points a game from here on out and pray that’s enough (and it might be!). The plight of both these teams has a few pundits wondering if the league should move the trade deadline to even later in the regular season, to which Arif Hasan and I say: Fuck that. Tough titty for you guys! WE GOT KIRK COUSINS AND YOU DIDN’T, NANNY NANNY BOO-BOO! That’s kinda the subject of this week’s episode .

items.title: How Much Better Can Matthew Schaefer Get?
items.author: Barry Petchesky
items.content:
Matthew Schaefer, the best NHL defenseman of the next generation and maybe already this one, is a pleasure to watch. The first unanimous Calder winner in 33 years, he finished second on the New York Islanders in both goals and assists last season. As a defenseman! As an 18-year-old! There is a damn teenager at the controls of the Isles' offense, driving play at both ends of the ice and looking so impossibly assured that he was named alternate captain in his second year, and nobody thinks this is weird or fluky. Sure, he was a no-brainer for first overall pick, but even wunderteens usually require some period of adjustment.

Year two has started even hotter. Twenty games in, Schaefer leads the Islanders in points (nine goals, 15 assists), all the while playing the fourth-most minutes per game of the entire league. Young legs are nice to have, but he's out here playing entire overtimes without coming off. His defense is good, if not quite elite—he's still vulnerable to being forechecked, and his positioning can sometimes be off—but the stage for the Schaefer Show is 200 feet long. He's a demon in transition and a menace in the offensive zone. "We're watching greatness kind of evolve," teammate Mathew Barzal said.

The most complimentary thing I can say about Schaefer's scoring is that he is not by any means a chucker. He's not perched at the blue line, clapping pucks on a prayer, like some empty-calorie offensive defensemen I could name. His very reasonable shot percentage both last year and this represent neither a player who has been especially lucky, nor a volume scorer taking away other, potentially shorter-odds opportunities. He is earning his points with his decisions.
